answer: A link-state algorithm is what's called a centralized or global routing algorithm, meaning every node has the complete picture of the network topology and all the link costs. Each router floods its link-state information so everyone ends up with the same map. Then each node independently runs something like Dijkstra's algorithm to compute the least-cost path to every other node. That's different from distance-vector, where a node only knows what its neighbors tell it and the computation is iterative and distributed.

If that order is T1 then T2, T1 will never see the inserted row.

answer: In a complete binary tree of depth d, every node at a level less than d minus 1 has two children. Also, if a node has a right descendant at level d, it must have a left child, and all its left descendants are either leaves or have two children, which means the bottom level fills strictly from left to right. Under that definition the last level ends up with an odd number of nodes, since it's filled left-first. So depth and node count are tied together: all the levels above are completely full, and the last level just holds the leftover nodes.

answer: With the Builder pattern, the class that needs a complex object, the director, doesn't assemble it itself; it delegates the creation to a builder object. All the step-by-step construction logic is encapsulated in that separate builder, so the director only calls steps like buildWalls and buildRoof. Because the director only talks to the builder interface, you can plug in different concrete builders and get different representations of the same complex object, like a stone house versus a wooden house, from the same construction process.

answer: MVC splits the application into three parts: the model holds the data and business logic, the view is what the user sees, and the controller handles user input. The controller sits between them as the intermediary, taking actions from the view, updating the model, and telling the view to refresh. Because of that, the graphical interface is fully decoupled from the code that handles user actions and data. The implication is that you can redesign the UI or add a mobile view without rewriting the business logic, and each part is easier to test and maintain.

answer: The three buckets basically correspond to three different questions you ask when designing. Creational patterns like Factory or Singleton are about how objects get created. Structural patterns like Adapter or Composite are about the static shape of the system, how classes and objects are composed into larger structures. Behavioral patterns like Observer or Strategy are about the dynamic side, how objects interact and split responsibilities at runtime. So the grouping pushes you to frame a design problem as a creation, structure or interaction problem and then pick from the right family.

answer: A logical address is the address the CPU generates when a program runs, and it's also called a virtual address. A physical address is the actual address seen by the memory unit, the one that goes out on the memory bus. With compile-time or load-time address binding, the logical and physical addresses are the same. They only differ with execution-time binding, where the MMU translates each logical address to a physical one at runtime.

answer: You number every resource, say the printer is 1, the disk is 2, the tape drive is 3, and make a rule that a process can only request resources in increasing order of those numbers. So if you hold the disk, you can ask for the tape drive but never go back and ask for the printer. That means you can never get a loop where A waits on B and B waits on A, because waiting always points toward higher numbers. Since circular wait is one of the four necessary conditions for deadlock, breaking it guarantees deadlock can't happen.

key_points: Processes must request resources in increasing order of their assigned numerical numbers.
This is one of the four conditions that must be violated to prevent deadlock.

answer: In round-robin, every time a process's quantum expires you get a context switch, so the time quantum directly controls how many switches happen. If the quantum is tiny, you spend a big chunk of CPU time just saving and restoring state, and the overhead dominates. In modern systems the quantum is chosen so the context switch time is a small fraction of it, microseconds for the switch versus tens of milliseconds for the quantum. Switches get much more expensive if they involve swapping processes in and out of memory. But if the quantum is too large, round-robin degenerates into FCFS and response time suffers, so it's a trade-off.

answer: Before granting a request, the Banker's algorithm pretends to grant it and then checks whether the system would still be safe. For the check, it keeps a Work vector that starts as the currently available resources, and a Finish flag for each process. It looks for any unfinished process whose remaining need fits within Work, pretends that process runs to completion and gives back everything it holds, so Work grows, and sets its Finish flag to true. If eventually every Finish entry is true, there's a safe sequence and the request is granted; otherwise the process has to wait.

answer: test_and_set is a hardware instruction that atomically reads a shared boolean and sets it to true in one indivisible step. It returns the original value, so a process spins on while test_and_set of lock, and if it gets back false, the lock was free and now it owns it. Because the operation is atomic, no other process can sneak in between the read and the write, so nobody else can grab the lock mid-operation. If two processes execute it at the same moment on different CPUs, the hardware serializes them, so only one gets false back and enters the critical section, while the other gets true and keeps spinning until the lock is released.
